clue.text: Preens: repeatedly improves make-up, plucks and shaves - just for starters!

definitions.text: Preens: repeatedly improves make-up, plucks and shaves

indicators.note: starters are what come at the beginning, so only the opening letter of each word is wanted

blocks.note: opening letter of this word
opening letter of this word
opening letter of this word
opening letter of this word
opening letter of this word
opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A description of someone fussing over their appearance in front of the mirror, touching up make-up and grooming.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue, minus the instruction at the end, both describes the answer and supplies its letters; 'and' is skipped as a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: To primp is to groom yourself fussily, which is exactly what someone fixing make-up, plucking brows and shaving is doing.

clue.text: Caught interrupting musical intro in bar

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a prelude is an introductory piece of music
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A cricket catch somehow breaking into the opening bars of a piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like part of the musical picture, but here it is a verb meaning prevent.
explanation.definitionFit: To preclude something is to rule it out or prevent it from happening, the verb sense of bar.

clue.text: Mischief-maker's solidarity bringing impossibility of punishment

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child or sprite; the 's means 'has'
solidarity is unity of purpose

explanation.surface: A gang of troublemakers sticking together so that none of them can be punished.
explanation.definitionFit: Impunity is exemption from penalty, being safe from any consequences for what one has done.

clue.text: Celebrate winter at the pond, drunk

indicators.note: someone drunk is muddled and unsteady, so the preceding words are jumbled up

blocks.note: the letters of these words, used as fodder

explanation.surface: A tipsy party out on a frozen pond in winter.
explanation.definitionFit: To paint the town red is an idiom for going out and celebrating wildly.

clue.text: Taken aback in lilac, I'm initially hostile

indicators.note: the letters are found sitting inside the run of words that follows
something taken aback is pushed backwards, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning these words

explanation.surface: Someone startled and turned unfriendly while wearing or standing among lilac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it only supplies letters to the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Inimical describes something unfriendly or harmful, like an enemy; it shares a root with enemy.

clue.text: Thieve where thieves are

blocks.note: first meaning: slang verb for steal
second meaning: British slang for prison or a police station

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, the nick is a police station or jail, where caught thieves end up.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal British for stealing something and also for the jail that holds convicted criminals.

clue.text: Safe place for dangerous drivers?

blocks.note: first meaning: moderate and unadventurous, avoiding extremes
second meaning, playfully: the centre of the carriageway, where reckless motorists straddle the white line

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, but it splits after 'Safe': a word for cautious and a literal spot on the road, with the question mark flagging the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes moderate, cautious opinions or tastes, and also literally names the centre of a street.

clue.text: French novelist is seen around quiet college grounds

indicators.note: one item is put around another, wrapping it on both sides

blocks.note: Albert Camus, author of The Outsider
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A French writer spotted wandering the peaceful grounds of a university.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the land and buildings of a university or college, its grounds.

clue.text: Servant given black eye endlessly

indicators.note: without its ends, the phrase loses its outermost letters and what is left inside is kept

blocks.note: the letters sitting inside this phrase once its first and last are dropped

explanation.surface: A servant who has been punched and given a shiner.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the first and last letters of the two-word phrase leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lackey is a servile attendant or footman, someone who serves another obsequiously.

clue.text: Unorthodox priest presents wit from France

indicators.note: unorthodox means not following the usual pattern, so the letters break their normal order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An unconventional clergyman showing off his humour from France.
explanation.definitionFit: Esprit is a French word, also used in English, for liveliness of mind and witty spirit.

clue.text: This person may be a professor: it's irrelevant

definitions.text: This person may be a professor

blocks.clueFragment: This person may be a professor
blocks.note: first meaning: a noun for a university scholar
second meaning: an adjective for a question of no practical importance

explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes that a professor's views are irrelevant; 'it's academic' is a stock phrase meaning it no longer matters.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a university teacher or scholar, and the adjective describes a point of only theoretical, not practical, interest.

clue.text: Reading-Paddington's home straits, approaching London primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the leading letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: Paddington Bear came from darkest Peru
opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A railway journey from Reading to Paddington station, the train in difficulties as it approaches London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home straits' reads as the last leg of the trip, but straits only gives its first letter. Paddington Bear, the children's book character, came from Peru; Reading and Paddington are stations on one line.
explanation.definitionFit: A perusal is a careful reading or examination of a text, so the noun matches reading.

clue.text: Unsettle, unsettle and make spectacles

indicators.note: to unsettle is to disturb, so the letters of the preceding word are thrown out of order

blocks.note: the first word, used as fodder

explanation.surface: Repeated disturbance that somehow produces a pair of glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word appears twice: the first copy is the letters, the second the instruction to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunettes is an old-fashioned term, from French, for a pair of eyeglasses.

clue.text: Appeal of 'hysterical' Laurel

indicators.note: someone hysterical is wildly out of control, so the name that follows is scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The charm of Stan Laurel, half of the comic double act, whose films were hysterically funny.
explanation.walkthrough: Stan Laurel was the thin half of Laurel and Hardy; the quotes on 'hysterical' hint at the sense of very funny.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is the quality of being attractive or tempting, the power to draw people in.

clue.text: Little saint getting on with putting on a show

blocks.note: ST is the short form of saint
getting on means growing old

explanation.surface: An elderly saint still mounting theatrical productions.
explanation.definitionFit: Staging is the act of producing and presenting a play or performance to an audience.

clue.text: Lots of Netherlanders?

blocks.note: surface reading: a great many people from the Netherlands
setter's reading: lots are items put up at a sale, and the sale is named after the Dutch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots' means numerous people until you read it as items under the hammer; a Dutch-style sale starts high and the price drops until someone bids.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch auction is a sale where the asking price is lowered step by step until a buyer accepts it.

clue.text: Sounds like the dolls are lined up to cook burgers, say

indicators.note: the instruction says to go by what is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: Barbie is a famous doll, and a line of waiting people is a queue

explanation.surface: A child's game of lining up dolls to grill a meal at a cookout.
explanation.definitionFit: To barbecue is to cook food such as burgers over an open grill outdoors; 'say' marks burgers as one example.

clue.text: Always tore around showing great respect

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one word goes on both sides of the other

blocks.note: rent is an old past tense of rend, to tear
ever can mean always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps tearing about the place, oddly while being deeply respectful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tore around' reads as rushing about, but tore is the outer word holding always.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverent describes feeling or showing deep, solemn respect, as for something sacred.

clue.text: Candid features? One gives nothing away

blocks.note: first meaning: honest, unbending features, playfully read
second meaning: an unreadable expression that hides your feelings

explanation.walkthrough: Straight can mean honest, so 'candid features' is a playful gloss; a poker player keeps an unrevealing expression.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan expression that betrays no amusement or emotion, literally an honest-looking or level countenance.

clue.text: Olympian team stinks, going after gold at first

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: the leading letter of this word
to stink is to reek

explanation.surface: A sports fan complaining that their Olympic squad is terrible, despite winning gold early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going after' places the second piece after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece hosted the ancient Olympic Games, so its people make a fitting Olympian team; Olympians were also Greek gods.

clue.text: Headlouse seen in school, briefly? I'm telling!

definitions.note: the cry of a telltale, standing for the telltale himself

indicators.note: something seen in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: SCH is a standard short form of school
a nit is the egg or young of a head louse

explanation.surface: A child spotting head lice at school and threatening to tell the teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A snitch is a telltale or informer, the kind of child who announces they are going to tell on someone.

clue.text: Makes born again, putting Bible classes before recent events

blocks.note: RE is religious education, a school subject in Britain
news is the report of recent events

explanation.surface: An evangelical revival, with scripture study taking priority over current affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to make it new again or restore it, so it is in effect reborn.

clue.text: The Arles together?

blocks.note: surface reading: perhaps a family named Arles gathered as a group
setter's reading: Arles is a town in France, so give the word the locals use for together

explanation.walkthrough: Arles is a city in Provence; the French word for together is also English for a group performing as one.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a group of musicians or actors performing together; in French the word simply means together.

clue.text: Globally evens out, revealing an end

indicators.note: the letters in even positions are thrown out, leaving the odd ones

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of this word

explanation.surface: Worldwide things balancing out to show a final purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: A goal is an aim or objective, the end one is working towards.

clue.text: Former husband, reformed rioter, is outside

indicators.note: something reformed has been reshaped, so the word after it is rearranged

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's ex, once a troublemaker but now reformed, has been released from prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The exterior is the outer surface or outside part of something, the opposite of interior.

clue.text: Seedy, the French housing? 'That hurts!'

indicators.note: housing means holding inside, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: le is a French word for the
the usual cry of pain

explanation.surface: A cry of pain from someone in a shabby lodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Louche means disreputable or of dubious morals, much like seedy in the sense of sleazy.

clue.text: 'You don't see loafers on this,' she'd clue cryptically

indicators.note: something written cryptically is disguised, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these words, used as fodder

explanation.surface: A setter boasting that her timetable leaves no room for idlers.
explanation.walkthrough: Loafers are idle people, who have no fixed timetable; 'loafers' tempts you towards shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A schedule is a timetable of planned tasks, and anyone who keeps to one is by definition not loafing.

clue.text: Most of December in commercial outlet

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial
a vent is an outlet for air or steam

explanation.surface: A shop advert running for nearly the whole Christmas season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' looks like a deletion instruction, but the whole phrase is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Advent is the church season of the four Sundays before Christmas, covering most of the final month.
